```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Where a camera sits shapes what it can detect and how its data can be pooled with others.
WildObsR places camera coordinates in their Australian context: the state or territory,
the IBRA bioregion, the nearest protected area, a metric map projection, and the spacing
between neighbouring cameras. The state, bioregion and protected-area layers ship with the
package, so everything here runs offline. This vignette uses the two Wet Tropics projects
bundled with WildObsR.

```{r data}
library(WildObsR)

# the two projects shipped with WildObsR
dp_list <- example_datapackages()

# one row per camera station, from both projects
deps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dp_list, function(dp) {
  dp$data$deployments[, c("deploymentID", "locationID", "locationName", "latitude", "longitude")]
}))
stations <- deps[!duplicated(deps$locationID), ]
rownames(stations) <- NULL
nrow(stations)
```

## State or territory

`AUS_state_locator()` adds the state or territory each camera falls in, from the `ozmaps`
boundaries. State matters because threatened-species listings, and so the obscuring of
public records, differ between states.

```{r state}
# the state of every station
stations <- AUS_state_locator(stations)
table(stations$state)
```

## IBRA bioregion and subregion

The Interim Biogeographic Regionalisation for Australia (IBRA 7) divides the continent into
89 bioregions and 419 subregions of similar climate, geology and vegetation. It is a common
unit for pooling surveys and for reporting.

```{r ibra}
# the bioregion and subregion of every station
stations <- ibra_classification(stations, lat_col = "latitude", long_col = "longitude")
table(stations$IBRAbioRegionName)
table(stations$IBRAsubRegionName)
```

## Protected areas

WildObs `locationName` values are usually a protected area. Two functions check them against
the Collaborative Australian Protected Areas Database (CAPAD 2022).
`locationName_verification_CAPAD()` names the protected area each camera is in, or the
nearest one and its distance in metres. `locationName_buffer_CAPAD()` draws a buffer around
each camera, merges buffers that overlap into one landscape, and names each landscape after
the protected area that covers most of it, which groups nearby cameras into the same unit.

```{r capad}
# a few stations from each project, to keep the example quick
few <- stations[c(1, 2, nrow(stations) - 1, nrow(stations)), ]

# the protected area each camera is in, or nearest to, beside the recorded locationName
verified <- locationName_verification_CAPAD(few)
verified[, c("locationID", "locationName", "CAPADlocationName", "CAPADminDistance")]

# cameras whose 1 km buffers overlap share a landscape, named by its main protected area
buffered <- locationName_buffer_CAPAD(few, buffer_size = 1000)
buffered[, c("locationID", "CAPADlocationNameBuffer")]
```

A recorded `locationName` can differ from the CAPAD name for good reasons. Where protected
areas overlap, curation gives each landscape one name. For example, the first Paluma camera
above is nearest the Girringun Indigenous Protected Area, which overlaps Paluma Range
National Park, and its landscape is recorded as the national park. A camera can also sit just outside a reserve
boundary, or a reserve can be recorded under a local name. Treat a difference as a prompt to
look, not as an error.

## Metric coordinates

Distances and grids need coordinates in metres. `UTM_coord_generator()` projects each
camera into the Universal Transverse Mercator zone its longitude falls in, and returns the
zone with the coordinates.

```{r utm}
# the UTM zone, easting (X) and northing (Y) in metres for every deployment
utm <- UTM_coord_generator(deps)
head(utm)
```

## Spacing between cameras

`find_nearest_neighbor_distance()` gives the distance from each station to its nearest
neighbour. Camera spacing decides whether neighbouring stations can be treated as
independent sites for a species with a given home range, and which grid cell size suits a
pooled analysis.

```{r spacing}
# the nearest other station to each station, and how far it is
nn <- find_nearest_neighbor_distance(deps)
# spacing in metres
summary(nn$distance)
```

```{r spacing-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Histogram of distances in metres from each camera station to its nearest neighbour."}
hist(nn$distance, breaks = 30, main = "Distance to the nearest camera station",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", col = "darkgreen", border = "white")
```

## Data sources

The CAPAD 2022 terrestrial and IBRA 7 subregion layers ship with WildObsR as the datasets
`capad` and `ibra`, simplified for size. Both are © Commonwealth of Australia (Department of
Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water), licensed under Creative Commons
Attribution. State boundaries come from the `ozmaps` package.
